# **Persona**

A representation of a user or stakeholder.  
Personas help ground architectural choices in real needs by modeling  
motivations, behaviours, and constraints.

Personas are useful for:
- system justification  
- narrative context  
- scope boundaries  
- human-centric design decisions

# Document Types

Documents come in several types, each representing a different kind of knowledge.  
The type influences structure, default sections, and how the document appears in  
navigation and architecture views.

Each document type still behaves like any other document: it has sections,  
metadata, lineage, and participates in the knowledge graph. The type simply  
anchors the document in a broader conceptual category.

# Problem statement

We need a consistent, relatable example system to explain the concepts of the notebook.
Without a shared demo system, documents—such as decisions, principles, sketches, diagrams, or narratives—risk becoming abstract or disconnected.

A good demo must:
	•	Be simple enough to understand quickly
	•	Be rich enough to cover all architectural concepts
	•	Contain real workflows that justify decisions
	•	Support C4 modeling, design decisions, principles, personas, and diagrams
	•	Provide stable context for examples, tutorials, and onboarding materials

Existing examples were either too trivial or too complex to serve this purpose.

# Decision

We introduce the Conference Registration App as the primary demo system within the notebook.

The system is deliberately scoped to:
	•	Allow users to browse sessions, register, pay, and manage their personal agenda
	•	Include organizers managing sessions, capacity, and speakers
	•	Integrate with external services (payment provider, email service)
	•	Provide meaningful boundaries suitable for a C4 model
	•	Enable a full set of architecture perspectives (functional, structural, behavioral, decision-making)

This system becomes the canonical example used in:
	•	Design decisions
	•	ADRs
	•	Principles
	•	Personas
	•	C4 diagrams
	•	Sketches and mermaid diagrams
	•	Embedded sections and narratives
	•	Search and knowledge graph demonstrations

Its stable domain and clear workflows make it ideal for showcasing how the notebook organizes and navigates architectural knowledge.

decision: Introduce a small but complete demo system—the Conference Registration App—to demonstrate all document types, perspectives, and architectural concepts within the notebook.

## Graph View

The graph view shows how documents relate to each other inside the notebook.  
Each document is a node in the knowledge graph. Edges represent structural  
relationships, such as:

- **parent of / child of** — the document hierarchy  
- **references** — explicit links defined in sections  
- **referenced by** — reverse relationships  

The selected document is shown as the central node.  
Its direct relationships—both inbound and outbound—are drawn around it,  
making the local structure easy to understand at a glance.

Use graph view to:

- explore the context of a document  
- discover related material  
- check whether references are consistent  
- understand how narratives, decisions, and notes connect  
- see how deeply a concept is used across the notebook

Graph view focuses on clarity: only first-degree relationships are shown,  
keeping the visualization readable even in large notebooks.



# Working On

The **Working On** perspective gives you a focused view of what you are actively creating, reviewing, or shaping.  
It cuts through the full notebook and shows only the documents that matter *right now*.

## What This Perspective Shows

The view groups documents by their current phase:

- **Drafts** — documents you are writing or refining  
- **Review** — documents ready for discussion  

It is intentionally minimal.  And ordered on "last updated" to show what is top of mind.


<button @click="microDoc = {};navigation='dashboard'" class="btn btn-primary">Open working on view</button>

# **Note**

A general-purpose document for capturing ideas, explanations, analysis,  
or contextual information. Notes are flexible and contain any mix of sections.

Use notes for:
- explanations  
- definitions  
- background context  
- observations or research

## Sketch Section

A Sketch section is a lightweight Draw.io diagram stored as an XML file (`<id>.xml`).  
It uses the same diagrams.net editor but is intended for quick, informal visuals:  
rough shapes, early ideas, exploratory structures, or temporary sketches that  
support thinking rather than formal documentation.

Unlike full architecture diagrams, a Sketch section is intentionally minimal.  
Its purpose is to capture early-stage concepts or illustrate an idea without  
committing to a polished layout. Because it’s still XML-based, it opens in the  
same editor and can later be refined, expanded, or promoted to a more formal diagram.

# The Document

A “document” is the fundamental unit of knowledge in the notebook.  
It represents a single idea, decision, explanation, or concept—small enough to stay focused, but rich enough to stand on its own.

## What Is a Document?

A document groups together multiple sections into one coherent whole.  
Each document has its own folder, metadata, tags, and lineage, making it easy to reference, navigate, and evolve over time.

## Sections

A document consists of independent sections—markdown, diagrams, images, references, or slides.  
Each section is stored as its own file, allowing fine-grained versioning and clean diffs.

## Why Keep Documents Small?

Small documents are easier to understand, maintain, and reuse.  
Instead of one long page, a set of focused documents keeps the structure modular and navigable.

## References

Documents can reference each other to express relationships:  
parent/child, precedents, influences, or cross-links.  
This creates a connected graph of knowledge rather than a linear wiki.

## Living Structure

Documents evolve over time.  
Each update is versioned, each section can be rewritten independently,  
and the system continuously rebuilds navigation, lineage, and search indexes.
# The sections
And the last section type is *embedding* and a lot of the above content is actually embedded sections from other documents.

## Embedded Section

An Embedded section lets a document display one or more sections from another  
document inline. Instead of linking or referencing a document, the embedded  
section pulls the actual rendered content from the target document and places it  
directly inside the current one. This is similar to how Infodecks can assemble  
slides from multiple sources — but here the layout is portrait and designed for  
reading rather than presenting.

Embedded sections are ideal for reusing content such as principles, ADR  
summaries, personas, or key diagrams without duplicating text. When the source  
document is updated, every embedded section automatically reflects the latest  
version. This keeps knowledge consistent across the entire notebook while still  
letting you structure the narrative however you prefer.

## Inline Reuse

An Embedded section lets you display parts of another document directly inside
the current one. It pulls the rendered content inline — no duplication, no
manual syncing.

This is ideal for reusing principles, ADR summaries, personas, or diagrams.
Updates to the source document automatically flow through, keeping everything
consistent while you shape the narrative however you like.

## Attendee (Persona)

**Role**  
Conference visitor who registers, pays, and participates in sessions during the event.

**Goals**  
- Quickly register and secure a ticket.  
- Receive clear confirmation of payment and attendance.  
- Access event information (agenda, speakers, venue).  
- Manage their own registration (updates, cancellations).

**Frustrations**  
- Confusing registration flows or too many required fields.  
- Unclear or delayed payment confirmation.  
- Last-minute changes not communicated properly.  
- Limited visibility into sessions they’ve signed up for.

**Needs from the System**  
- A simple, mobile-friendly registration form.  
- Reliable payment processing with immediate confirmation.  
- Automated email notifications (ticket, updates).  
- Ability to update profile or cancel without manual support.

# The Narrative

This deck introduces the core concepts step by step, showing how each idea connects to the next.  
It’s a guided path through the essentials—clear, concise, and focused on understanding the system as a whole.

## Reuse knowledge

The section on the right references a section from another note.Click the link to view the complete note.

Explore it freely — you can always return to this narrative.A **Back to Deck** button will appear in the menu bar, taking you straight back to the exact slide where you left off.

You can use decks to create a standalone narrative, but this deck takes a different role:it guides you through the notes, gives you clear entry points, and helps you navigate the documentation in a structured way.

sections.data:
# **ADR (Architecture Decision Record)**

A formal, structured decision record based on established ADR templates.  
ADRs capture long-term architectural decisions, including alternatives,  
considerations, consequences, and trade-offs.

ADRs provide:
- durable architectural memory  
- traceability  
- rationale and alternatives  
- consistent structure across teams

## Additional Structure in ADRs

In this notebook, ADRs also include two explicit elements:
	•	Effect — describes the architectural impact of the decision
(e.g., introduces a new system).
	•	Y-statement — a concise, structured justification capturing
In the context of … facing … we decided for … and discarded … to achieve … accepting the consequence of ….

These additions make ADRs more actionable and ensure their impact is reflected across perspectives, lineage, and architectural views.

# ADR as a Tool for Managing Technical Debt

In this notebook, ADRs can also be used to explicitly register technical debt.
Technical debt should always be a conscious, justified choice — never an accident or an undocumented shortcut.
By capturing technical debt as an ADR:
	•	the rationale behind the compromise is recorded,
	•	the context and constraints are preserved,
	•	the intended follow-up or remediation path is made explicit, and
	•	teams avoid “invisible” architectural drift.

Framing technical debt as a decision ensures it receives the same level of scrutiny, traceability, and architectural visibility as any other significant choice.
This prevents unintentional erosion of the system and helps future teams understand why something was deferred, what was accepted, and under which conditions it should be resolved.

sections.data:
## Relationships

Every document participates in the knowledge graph through explicit and  
structural relationships. The right-hand sidebar shows two lists:

---

### Incoming Relationships

These are connections **pointing toward this document**.

Examples:

- **referenced by** — another document links to this one  
- **child of** — this document sits under a parent document  
- **guided by / linked from / preceded by** (depending on effect types)

Incoming relationships help you understand *who depends on this document*  
and where it appears in the wider notebook structure.

---

### Outgoing Relationships

These are connections **originating from this document**.

Examples:

- **references** — this document links to others  
- **parent of** — this document is the parent of another  
- **links to / guides / introduces** (for effect‐based relationships)

Outgoing relationships show *what this document relies on*, reuses, or  
contributes to in the knowledge graph.

---

Together, the incoming and outgoing lists give a complete picture of how  
a document fits into the notebook: its context, dependencies, and impact.

sections.data:
## Status: Deleted

Setting the status of a document to **deleted** does not remove it from the notebook.

Instead, the document becomes **archived**:

- it disappears from the navigation tree  
- it no longer appears in Search  
- it can still be included when **Search archive** is enabled  
- it remains as a node in the knowledge graph (so relationships stay intact)

A “deleted” document is never lost automatically. It is simply hidden.

## Archived Documents

An archived document behaves like a soft-deleted item.  
It is still physically present in the notebook folder, including:

- its `index.json`  
- all associated section files  
- relationships  
- tags  
- metadata  

Archived documents are useful for keeping historical context without cluttering the active structure.

Because they remain in the graph, they continue to express lineage, references, and impact—even when hidden from day-to-day navigation.

## Permanent Deletion

Archived documents can be **permanently removed**.

Permanent deletion:

- removes the document’s directory from disk  
- removes all section files  
- updates indices and search caches  
- removes the node from the knowledge graph  

This action cannot be undone.

You typically use permanent deletion when:

- the content is obsolete  
- it was a placeholder or experiment  
- you want to remove sensitive or incorrect material  
- the document’s historical value is no longer needed

## Reference Cleanup Before Deletion

Before you permanently delete a document, you must remove all references **manually**.

The notebook does *not* automatically update or remove:

- reference sections pointing to the document  
- slide embeds that include the document  
- parent/child relationships  
- precedent / guided-by relations  
- design-link edges  
- architectural link effects

If you delete a document that still has inbound or outbound references,
those references will remain in other documents and will point to a non-existent target.

This can create broken links in:

- the knowledge graph  
- infodecks  
- tables of lineage  
- search results  
- embedded or referenced sections

Always clean up references first.

# Metadata

Metadata describes the “shape” of a document—what it is, where it belongs, and how it evolves.  
While the content communicates ideas, metadata communicates structure.

## What Metadata Does

Metadata helps the notebook understand how a document fits into the larger whole.  
It supports navigation, lineage, organization, and cross-referencing.

Without metadata, a notebook would be a flat pile of notes.  
With it, the system becomes a navigable and expressive knowledge graph.

## Types of Metadata

A document contains multiple categories of metadata that work together to define its role, behavior, and context.

### Document Identity

Each document carries a small set of fields that establish its identity:

- **id** — unique folder name  (not visible in UI)
- **name** — human-readable title  
- **type** — the kind of document this is (e.g., note, ADR, persona, infodeck)

These attributes help both humans and the system understand the document’s purpose.

### Lifecycle

The lifecycle indicates how “ready” a document is for consumption.  
Common lifecycle states include:

- **draft**  
- **published**  
- **decided**  
- **deprecated**

Lifecycle metadata helps you keep track of which documents are authoritative and which are still evolving. 

### Structure

Structural metadata defines how documents relate to one another:

- **parent** — narrative hierarchy  
- **precedent** / **effect** — architectural relationships  
- **scope** — optional architectural level (landscape / system / container / component)

These fields shape both the tree and the graph views.

### Classification

Classification metadata helps you organize and filter documents:

- **tags** — free-form labels  
- **persona**, **principle**, or **effect** — depending on the document type  

This makes it easy to build cross-cutting groups and thematic clusters.

### Timing

Documents track their own history using two timestamps:

- **created**  
- **updated**

Timing metadata supports sorting, export, reviews, and understanding how a document evolved.

## Why Metadata Matters

Metadata allows you to:

- navigate large notebooks more easily  
- trace how ideas evolve across time  
- assemble narrative structures 
- generate C4 diagrams 
- filter by tags, type, or status  
- generate the knowledge graph  

Metadata isn’t decoration—it's the structural backbone that makes the notebook coherent and scalable.

# Problem statement

The Conference Registration App requires a secure, compliant payment solution capable of handling international attendees.
If we process payments ourselves using a traditional PSP (Stripe, Mollie, Adyen, etc.), we must:
	•	become the legal merchant of record,
	•	register for VAT in every jurisdiction,
	•	issue compliant invoices,
	•	handle chargebacks,
	•	manage fraud screening,
	•	comply with regional consumer protections,
	•	maintain financial audit trails.

This is high cost, high risk, and outside the scope of the demo system.

We want a payment solution that eliminates operational friction and provides a realistic integration example without distracting from the architectural concepts.

# Decision

We adopt Paddle as the Merchant of Record.

Paddle handles:
	•	all taxes (VAT/GST/consumption tax)
	•	invoicing
	•	fraud & chargebacks
	•	refunds
	•	compliance
	•	multi-currency support
	•	legal merchant responsibilities
	•	payment infrastructure and billing logic

Our backend will:
	•	initiate a Paddle checkout session,
	•	wait for the webhook callback,
	•	mark registration as paid,
	•	issue the digital conference ticket.

This provides a realistic, low-friction payment flow ideal for a demo architecture.

ystatement.context: Building the Conference Registration App, where users must be able to purchase conference tickets online
ystatement.concern: Regulatory complexity (VAT, international tax handling, invoicing), fraud risks, chargebacks, financial reporting obligations, and the legal responsibilities associated with processing payments as a first-party merchant.
ystatement.decision: Using Paddle as our Merchant of Record (MoR)—delegating taxation, invoicing, compliance, fraud management, and global payment operations to Paddle’s platform.
ystatement.alternatives:
•	Building our own payment processing flow (Stripe direct integration)
Too much compliance overhead and business risk.

•	Using a PSP only (e.g. Mollie/Adyen/Stripe w/out MoR)
Still requires us to be legally responsible for VAT, refunds, and invoicing.

•	Local-only payment tools
Not feasible for an international audience.
ystatement.quality: A simple, compliant, globally available checkout experience that requires minimal legal or operational burden on our side, while enabling experimentation with pricing, promotions, and subscription-based features.
ystatement.consequence:
•	Being tied to Paddle’s workflow, receipt formats, and refund APIs

•	Having less flexibility in deeply customized checkout flows

•	Relying on Paddle’s availability and policies

•	Paying a higher fee compared to PSP-only providers

•	Adjusting backend workflows to Paddle’s “transaction → fulfillment” model

## Technical Debt Justification
We explicitly mark this as **intentional technical debt**.  
The simplified engine helps communicate architectural intent (event-sourcing, append-only log, projections) without requiring the reader to understand a full production system.  
A future implementation **must** introduce the missing safeguards, validation, and tooling.

# Decision

Describe the decision that is taken...

ystatement.context: Building a demo-friendly, easy-to-understand version of the Reservation Service using event-sourcing concepts.
ystatement.concern:
The complexity and effort required to implement a production-grade event engine:
- schema versioning and migrations  
- correct idempotency behavior  
- replay safety and replay speed  
- concurrency handling  
- snapshotting and compaction  
- fine-grained error handling and recovery
ystatement.decision: A **minimal, simplified Event Engine** that accepts and emits events without enforcing schema validation, migration rules, idempotency checks, or replay guarantees.
ystatement.alternatives:
- A fully validated, versioned event schema registry  
- Snapshotting to prevent unbounded replay times  
- Race-condition handling through optimistic concurrency controls  
- Automated migration and projection rebuild tooling  
- Guarantees for backward- and forward-compatibility
ystatement.quality:

# Search

The **Search** perspective helps you find documents and sections across the entire notebook.
It gives you a fast, unified way to navigate your knowledge—no matter where content lives.



## What Search Covers

Search looks across all content within the notebook:

- document titles  
- markdown sections  
- metadata fields  
- tags  

Even archived content can be included when you enable **Search archive**.



## Knowledge Graph Preview

Search shows a miniature **knowledge graph** of the matching documents.

- Orange nodes represent documents matching your search.  
- Blue nodes represent related documents.  
- Edges show referencing relationships.

This helps you understand how results relate to the rest of the notebook.

## Filtering With Tags

You can narrow search results using tags.

- Click a tag to activate it  
- Activate multiple tags at once  
- Remove individual filters or clear all

This makes Search work both as a query tool *and* a lightweight faceted browser.

## Search Archive

By default, Search only looks at active documents.
Turning on **Search archive** switches to archived items.
This is helpful when you need prior context or want to revive older thinking.

## When to Use Search

Search is especially helpful when:

- you don’t remember where a document lives  
- you want to find all content related to a topic  
- you want to explore your notebook semantically  
- you want a graph-based overview of related documents  
- you're working across many parallel threads  

Search acts as your “global entry point” into the notebook.

## Design Intent

The notebook encourages small documents and many connections.
The **Search** perspective complements this by providing:

- full-text discovery  
- semantic navigation  
- graph-based contextual awareness  

Instead of browsing deep structures, you jump directly to what you need.
<button @click="microDoc = {};navigation='search'" class="btn btn-primary">Open search</button>

# Last Opened

The **Last Opened** perspective gives you quick access to the documents you recently interacted with.
It helps you pick up your work exactly where you left off.



## What This Perspective Shows

This view lists your most recently opened documents, regardless of their type:

- notes  
- decisions  
- principles  
- narratives  

Every time you open a document, it moves to the top of this list.

## Why This Perspective Exists

When working across multiple threads—architecture, decisions, diagrams, narratives—it’s easy to lose track of your last context.

The *Last Opened* perspective:

- gives you a lightweight “jump back” history  
- reduces the need to navigate through folders  
- supports fast switching between documents  
- mirrors how you naturally move through ideas

## How It Works

This perspective is automatically maintained:

- Every opened document is added to history.  
- Opening it again moves it to the top.  
- Deleted documents disappear from the list.  
- The list persists across sessions.

You don’t need to curate it manually.

name: Component Separation Principle
principle:
### Statement
To maintain a clean separation of concerns, the Conference Management system separates **presentation**, **application**, and **integration** responsibilities into distinct components.

### Rationale
Clear boundaries between UI components (Registration, Admin Console), backend services (Reservation Service), and external integrations (Paddle as Merchant of Record) reduce coupling and improve evolvability.  
This ensures that UI changes do not affect backend logic, backend changes do not break integrations, and external providers can be swapped with minimal disruption.  
It also supports independent deployment pipelines and simplifies operational ownership.

### Implication / Acceptance
We accept that maintaining multiple components introduces additional integration work, such as defining explicit APIs and event contracts.  
We also accept that troubleshooting may require coordination across components, but this trade-off is justified by improved maintainability and long-term agility.

# The Demo Application

The Demo Application is a small, fictional system designed to showcase how the notebook models architectural knowledge.  
It is intentionally simple, but rich enough to demonstrate **all document types**, **architecture perspectives**,  
and **the way knowledge flows through the notebook**.

---

## Purpose of the Demo

The goal of the demo is not to model a real product, but to provide a clear, shared reference.  
Every concept in the notebook can point to the demo application—from principles to ADRs,  
personas, diagrams, and narratives.  

It acts as the “playground architecture” where each document type can be demonstrated  
in a realistic but safe context.

## Draw.io Section

A Draw.io section stores a diagram created with the diagrams.net (Draw.io) editor.  
Each diagram is saved as an XML file (`<id>.xml`) inside the document’s folder.  
The XML format contains both the structural graph data and the visual layout information,  
allowing the editor to fully reconstruct the diagram whenever you reopen it.

Draw.io sections are ideal for expressing architectures, workflows,  
context boundaries, or any concept that benefits from visual structure  
rather than pure text.

## Why Use Draw.io Sections?

Visual reasoning is often more efficient than textual description.  
A Draw.io section creates a shared mental model by showing relationships,  
dependencies, and boundaries explicitly rather than describing them in prose.  
This is especially useful when documenting architecture,  
design decisions, system interactions, and domain concepts.

Because diagrams are stored separately as XML, they can be versioned,  
diffed, and evolved over time without interfering with the rest of the document.  
This makes them stable building blocks within your narrative or decision record.

## Storage Format

Each Draw.io section corresponds to a single XML file located in the document's directory.  
The filename matches the section’s `id`, ensuring predictable lookup and easy referencing.  
The XML contains the full diagram state, including shapes, connections, styles,  
metadata, and editor-specific configuration.

Storing diagrams as standalone XML files allows them to be reused, exported,  
or embedded without altering the main document structure.  
It also makes it straightforward to process or migrate diagrams programmatically.

## Editing the Diagram

When you open a Draw.io section, the editor loads its associated XML file  
through the local file system. You can modify the diagram just like in  
the standard diagrams.net interface—adding nodes, rearranging layout,  
changing colors, or annotating relationships.

Saving the diagram writes the updated XML back to the same file.  
This ensures that the diagram remains perfectly in sync with the rest of the notebook,  
and can be referenced reliably from slides, principles, ADRs, or other documents.

## Referencing Diagrams

Draw.io sections can be referenced by other documents or slides simply by ID.  
This allows a single authoritative diagram to be reused across multiple contexts  
without duplicating files or risking divergence.

In narrative decks, you can place a Draw.io section inside a slide to illustrate  
the concept being explained. In ADRs or principles, you can reference a diagram  
to show architectural consequences or system-level boundaries.  
This promotes consistency and reduces maintenance work across your documentation.

# **Design Decision**

A lightweight structured record of a design choice.  
Design decisions describe a problem and the chosen solution, but remain  
less formal than an ADR.

Design decisions focus on:
- the problem  
- the decision  
- the reasoning  
- the impact

## 🧩 Design Decisions and Architectural Effect

While a Design Decision is lighter and less formal than an ADR,
it can still have a direct impact on the architecture.

Some decisions introduce a new building block, reshape boundaries between components, or retire part of the system. Others adjust behaviour, responsibilities, or flows without changing structure.
To capture this impact explicitly, each Design Decision includes an Effect section.

The Effect describes:
	•	what the decision introduces, modifies, or removes,
	•	at which architectural level (system, container, component),
	•	whether its influence is internal or external, and
	•	which system or subsystem is affected.

This ensures that even lightweight decisions are traceable within the architectural landscape, without requiring the full formality of an ADR.

An example of a **design decision** is referenced below:

## Table Section

A Table section stores structured rows and columns of data in a simple JSON file  
(`<id>.json`). Unlike a Data section, which is optimized for chart-based  
visualization, a Table section focuses purely on tabular representation.  

Table sections are ideal for checklists, comparison matrices, configuration  
summaries, reference data, or any content where a clean table communicates  
better than prose. Because the underlying data is plain JSON, it remains  
easy to diff, version, or generate programmatically. The table UI renders  
the JSON directly and supports scrolling, fixed headers, and optional  
formatting while keeping the original dataset untouched.

## Architecture Perspective

The C4 diagram is the primary navigation model.  
Zooming in or out automatically filters all other architecture perspectives (Principles, Decisions, Technical Debt, Notes) based on relevance.

### Principles (list grows when drilling down)
Each principle has a defined scope:
- **N1 (System Context):** EAP  
- **N2 (Containers):** EAP + SAP  
- **N3 (Components):** EAP + SAP + CAP  

The deeper you zoom, the more principles apply.

### Decisions & Technical Debt (list shrinks when drilling down)
Items are shown only if their scope overlaps with the selected C4 level:
- N1 items appear at all levels  
- N2 items appear at N2 and N3  
- N3 items appear only at N3  

Zooming in shows fewer but more specific items.

### Notes
Notes follow the same scoping rules and only appear when relevant to the selected element.

## Mermaid Section

A Mermaid section stores a text-based diagram written in Mermaid syntax  
(`flowchart`, `sequenceDiagram`, `classDiagram`, `stateDiagram`, etc.).  
Instead of an XML file like Draw.io, a Mermaid section is saved as a simple  
Markdown-like text file (`<id>.mmd`), making it easy to read, edit, and version.  
The diagram is rendered dynamically in the UI whenever the section is viewed.

Mermaid sections are ideal for lightweight diagrams that benefit from being  
expressed as code: sequences, flows, small graphs, or conceptual maps.  
They are quick to create and easy to maintain, and because the source is plain  
text, they can be diffed and refactored just like any other part of your  
documentation.

## Section Archive

Sections are individual files inside a document.  
When a section is deleted, it is *not* removed from disk immediately.  
Instead, it moves into the **section archive**, where it can be reviewed, restored,  
or permanently removed.



### Why Sections Are Archived

Archiving protects against accidental loss.  
Sections may contain important diagrams, slides, images, or text that you may  
want to reuse later. The archive gives you a safe place to store these without  
cluttering the main document.

---

### What You Can Do in the Archive

Each archived section provides two actions:

- **Restore** — return the section to the document’s section list  
- **Delete permanently** — remove the underlying file from disk

Restoring brings the section back exactly as it was, including its content,  
metadata.

Permanent deletion is irreversible.

---

### When to Use the Archive

Use the archive when:

- a section is no longer relevant to the current narrative  
- you want to simplify the document without losing past work  
- you are iterating on diagrams, visuals, or markdown versions  
- you want a clean main document but keep optional material nearby

The archive keeps documents tidy while preserving history and options.

sections.data:
## Ordering Sections

A document is composed of multiple independent sections—each stored as its own  
file inside the document’s folder. The *Order Sections* view lets you rearrange  
these sections to control how the document is presented.



### How Ordering Works

- Every section (markdown, diagram, image, table, etc.) appears as a separate row.  
- You can move sections **up** or **down** to change their position.  
- The preview inside each row shows the actual content, helping you understand  
  what you are moving.
- The internal file structure does not change—only the order in the document  
  metadata is updated.

### Why Ordering Matters

The order determines how readers experience your document:

- The introduction appears at the top  
- Supporting content follows  
- Diagrams, visuals, and references can be positioned where they add the most clarity  
- Archived or reference-heavy sections can be placed near the end  

Keeping sections small and reorderable helps you refine narrative flow without  
rewriting or restructuring your content.

### After Reordering

Once the new order is saved:

- The reading view updates immediately  
- Navigation, lineage, and export functions reflect the new sequence  
- Infodecks and embedded sections use the updated ordering when referencing the document

Reordering gives you full control over the narrative flow while preserving the  
modular nature of each section.

# Narratives

A *narrative* is a structured, guided explanation.  
Where individual documents focus on a single idea, a narrative weaves multiple documents together into a coherent story.

The Narratives view shows an overview of all story-driven material in the notebook.

## Navigation

From the overview you can:

- Open a narrative  
- View its individual slides  
- Review its sections in context  
- See its relationships in the knowledge graph  
- Create a new infodeck

Narratives help you connect concepts, decisions, principles, and visuals into a unified explanation—while keeping the underlying documents small, modular, and maintainable.


<button @click="microDoc = {};navigation='infodecks'" class="btn btn-primary">Open narratives overview</button>

# Perspectives

A Perspective is a filtered view of the notebook—showing only the documents  
that matter for a specific question, audience, or investigation.  
Perspectives do not change the documents themselves; they simply choose *which*  
documents to show, and *how* they relate.

## Markdown Sections

A **markdown section** is the most common type of content block inside a document.  
It allows you to write free-form text using standard Markdown syntax, making it ideal for:

- explanations  
- notes  
- narrative content  
- decisions and rationale  
- examples and walkthroughs  
- long-form documentation

### Purpose

Markdown sections provide flexibility without sacrificing structure.  
Each section is stored as a separate file inside the document folder:

```
/<document-id>/
  index.json
  intro.md
  explanation.md
  conclusion.md
```

This ensures:
- clean diffs in Git  
- conflict-free merges  
- easy editing  
- small storage units  
- independence between sections  

### Editing

When you click on a markdown section, it opens a rich text area.  
You can type plain Markdown, including:

- **Bold**
- *Italic*
- `Inline code`
- ```code blocks```
- Lists
- Headings
- Links
- Images

The system automatically adjusts the textarea height and live-updates the preview.

### Saving

When you save the document:
- the Markdown content is written to a file named `<section-id>.md`
- the section definition in `index.json` is updated
- metadata such as `updated` timestamps are refreshed

Only the Markdown file changes, not the entire document, which keeps version history clean.

### Ordering

Markdown sections can be reordered within a document.  
The order in the `sections` array inside `index.json` determines how they appear in the UI.

### When to Use Markdown Sections

Use a markdown section when you need:

- descriptive text  
- conceptual explanations  
- architectural reasoning  
- tutorial steps  
- narrative storytelling  
- decision details  
- long-form writing  

If you need references, diagrams, slides, or embedded components, consider using other section types alongside markdown.

---
Markdown sections are the backbone of most documents.  
They strike a balance between expressiveness, version control friendliness, and structural clarity.

> The next section is meant as an excerpt to use in a slide, and to act as an anchor to link to.

This is an example of Markdown section, but there are other utilities provided:

| - | - | - |

| Image | HTML | Embed |

## HTML Section

An HTML section stores raw HTML content inside a standalone file  
(`<id>.html`). Unlike Markdown, which is rendered through a formatter,  
an HTML section gives you full control over structure, styling, and

This keeps the document flexible while preserving safety and  
maintaining a clear separation from other section types.

name: Component Encapsulation Within a Container
principle:
### Statement
All components inside the *Reservation Service* container must be **fully encapsulated**, exposing functionality only through their defined interfaces or events, and never accessing each other’s data or internals directly.

### Rationale
A container hosts multiple technical components (e.g., Configuration, Registration, Event Engine), each responsible for a distinct part of the domain workflow.  
To keep the container maintainable, components must interact only via stable contracts—such as service calls or domain events—preventing hidden coupling and accidental dependence on internal implementation details.  
This preserves the long-term autonomy of components, supports independent evolution, and makes failures easier to reason about.

### Implication / Acceptance
We accept that components may require explicit coordination via event contracts or shared service boundaries, even when running in the same container.  
We also accept minor performance overhead compared to direct access, but this trade-off ensures clearer ownership, reduces regressions, and enables components to be extracted into separate deployables if needed in the future.

## Data Section

A Data section stores structured information — usually metrics, timelines,  
or categorical values — that can be visualized as either a chart or a table.  
The raw data is saved as a JSON file (`<id>.json`) inside the document folder.  
When opened, the UI renders the dataset using a built-in Charts.js renderer,  
or falls back to a simple tabular view if no chart type is configured.

Data sections are ideal for showing trends, comparisons, distributions,  
or numeric insights that support the surrounding narrative.  
Because the underlying representation is just JSON, the dataset can be  
edited, generated, exported, or consumed by other tools.  
The visual rendering is ephemeral — the JSON is the source of truth —  
making Data sections easy to version, extend, or reuse across slides and documents.

# Organizer (Persona)

## Role
Responsible for planning, managing, and running the conference. Coordinates registration, tracks attendees, and monitors event logistics.

## Goals
* Ensure a smooth registration and check-in experience.
* Access accurate attendee lists at all times.
* Manage cancellations, updates, and payment confirmations efficiently.
* Monitor ticket sales, capacity, and session popularity.

## Frustrations
* Manual spreadsheets that become outdated quickly.
* Payment confirmations that arrive late or inconsistently.
* No real-time overview of registrations.
* High pressure during event-day check-in.

## Needs from the System
* Reliable registration workflow.
* Up-to-date attendee data at any moment.
* Integration with payment provider (e.g., Paddle as Merchant of Record).
* Clear dashboards & automated notifications.

## Image Section

An Image section stores a standalone image file inside the document folder.  
Images are saved in their original format (`.webp`, `.png`, `.jpg`, …) using the  
filename `<id>.<extension>`. Unlike diagrams or sketches, an Image section does  
not contain structured or editable content — it simply represents a static visual  
asset that the document can reference. The viewer loads the image directly from  
the file system and displays it at its natural resolution.

Image sections are ideal for screenshots, UI mockups, photos, annotated diagrams,  
or any visual reference that supports the narrative. Because the image exists as  
a real file, it can be replaced, optimized, versioned, or exported without  
affecting the rest of the document. Slides and other documents may also reuse  
the same image by referencing its section ID, ensuring consistency and avoiding  
duplication.





name: Cloud-Managed Services Over Self-Hosting
principle:
## Statement

To maximize reliability and focus engineering effort on business value, we prefer cloud-managed services over self-hosted infrastructure whenever a managed alternative meets our functional and regulatory requirements.

## Rationale

Cloud-managed services reduce operational burden, eliminate undifferentiated heavy lifting, and provide mature capabilities—such as scaling, patching, backups, and failover—out-of-the-box.
This allows teams to spend their limited engineering capacity on domain problems instead of running and maintaining commodity infrastructure.
Managed services also improve security posture through consistent updates, tested configurations, and responsibility-sharing models with the cloud provider.
In practice, they increase delivery velocity, reduce MTTR, and improve cost predictability over time.


## Implication / Acceptance

We accept that adopting managed services may introduce provider dependencies or proprietary operational models.
We accept that deep customization or low-level control may be limited compared to self-hosted solutions.
We also accept that certain workloads with specialized performance, regulatory, or data-sovereignty constraints may still require dedicated hosting — but these must be the exception, justified explicitly, and revisited periodically.
